title: Alcohol Face Bloating: Why You Look Puffy After Drinking and Fixes
excerpt: Why your face looks puffy and your stomach feels bloated after drinking, what actually helps the next morning, which drinks bloat you least, and when swelling is a reason to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why alcohol makes your face puffy and stomach bloated, how to get rid of it fast, which drinks bloat least, and when swelling needs a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a puffy face and a bloated stomach the morning after drinking are very common, and for a social drinker they're usually harmless and gone within a day. Most of the puffiness comes from fluid going to the wrong places: alcohol makes you lose water, salty food and drinks make your body hold on to what's left, and lying flat all night lets that fluid settle in your face and around your eyes. Stomach bloating has a different cause: alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and carbonated drinks like beer and hard seltzer add a lot of gas. This guide explains each cause in plain words, what actually helps the next morning, how to drink in a way that bloats you less, and the signs that swelling is something more than a hangover.

**The quick fixes:** Drink water steadily through the morning. Eat potassium-rich food such as a banana, potatoes, avocado, or yogurt, and go easy on salt. Put something cold on your face for a few minutes. Get moving, even a short walk. For stomach bloat, skip fizzy drinks, sip peppermint or ginger tea, and eat small, plain meals. Most people look and feel back to normal by the afternoon or the next day.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** swelling affects your lips, tongue, or throat, you have trouble breathing or swallowing, or you get hives with dizziness. These are signs of a serious allergic reaction. **Get urgent care if** you have severe stomach pain (especially pain that spreads to your back), you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, or your stools are black. **See a doctor soon if** facial puffiness doesn't go away after a couple of days, swelling is only on one side or comes with pain, warmth, or fever, your ankles, legs, or belly are swelling too, or your skin or eyes look yellow. If you drink every day and feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor rather than trying to manage it alone.

## Why Your Face Looks Puffy After Drinking

"Alcohol bloating face" is one of the most searched hangover complaints, and it makes sense once you know that your face is one of the first places extra fluid shows up. The skin around your eyes and cheeks is thin and loose, so even a small amount of fluid sitting in the tissue makes a visible difference. Several things stack up on a night out.

### 1. Alcohol makes you lose water, then your body overcorrects

Alcohol blocks a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone, or ADH). Vasopressin normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, you pee more than you drink, which is why the bathroom line at any bar is long. By the end of the night you're usually somewhat dehydrated.

Here's the part that surprises people. Dehydration doesn't make you look shrunken. Once the alcohol wears off, your body tries to rebalance by holding on to water and salt. Fluid shifts around between your blood vessels and the tissues, and some of it ends up sitting under the skin instead of where it's useful. The result is that you can feel thirsty and look swollen at the same time.

### 2. Salt pulls water into your tissues

Think about what usually goes with drinking: chips, fries, pizza, wings, a late-night kebab, salted rims on margaritas, and mixers like tomato juice in a Bloody Mary. That's a lot of sodium in a short time. Your body keeps the sodium in your blood within a tight range, so when you take in a lot of salt, it holds on to extra water to dilute it. Some of that water ends up in your tissues, and the face is where you see it first.

This is why the sodium and electrolyte angle matters more than most people expect. The puffiness often isn't from the alcohol alone. It's alcohol plus a salty meal plus not enough plain water.

### 3. Alcohol widens your blood vessels

Alcohol relaxes and widens blood vessels near the skin. That's what gives some people a warm, flushed look while drinking. Wider vessels can let a little more fluid leak into the surrounding tissue, which adds to the swollen, red look of a "drinker's face" the next morning. People who flush strongly after a small amount of alcohol may have a genetic difference in how they process alcohol, which we cover in our [guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive).

### 4. Gravity and bad sleep

When you're upright, gravity helps drain fluid from your face during the day. When you lie flat for hours, especially face-down, fluid pools in the loose tissue around your eyes and cheeks. On top of that, alcohol disrupts the second half of the night's sleep. You might be in bed for eight hours but get fewer hours of good rest, which on its own tends to leave people with puffy eyes and dark circles.

### 5. Inflammation and histamine

Alcohol triggers a mild inflammatory response in the body, and its breakdown product, acetaldehyde, is irritating to tissues. Some drinks, especially red wine and some beers, also contain histamine and related compounds. In people who are sensitive to them, these can cause flushing, a stuffy nose, and a bit of swelling. If you notice that one type of drink reliably makes your face puffier than others, a histamine sensitivity is one possible reason.

### Why it's worse in some people than others

Puffiness varies a lot from person to person. Things that tend to make it worse include:

- **Drinking more, or drinking faster,** which means more fluid loss and more of everything above
- **Eating a very salty meal** with your drinks or afterward
- **Drinking on an empty stomach**, which raises your blood alcohol faster
- **Sleeping face-down** or without a pillow
- **Hormonal changes**, since many women notice more fluid retention at certain points in their cycle
- **Getting older**, as skin becomes less elastic and fluid shows up more around the eyes

## Why Your Stomach Bloats After Drinking

"Bloating after drinking" usually means a tight, full, gassy belly, either during the night or the next morning. That's a different process from a puffy face, though the two often show up together.

### Carbonation is the biggest culprit

Beer, hard seltzer, sparkling wine, champagne, and spirits mixed with soda or tonic all bring carbon dioxide gas into your stomach. Some of it comes back up as burps, but some moves on into your intestines. A few rounds of a carbonated drink can mean a lot of swallowed gas. If you've ever felt like a balloon after a night of beer, this is most of the reason.

### Beer has extra fermentable carbs

Beer also contains carbohydrates from grain that aren't fully digested. When they reach your large intestine, gut bacteria ferment them and make more gas. This is one reason people talk about "beer bloat" in particular. Sweet mixers, sugary cocktails, and some ciders can do something similar, especially in people who are sensitive to certain sugars.

### Alcohol irritates the stomach lining

Alcohol is an irritant to the lining of the stomach. Heavier drinking can cause gastritis, which means inflammation of the stomach lining. That can feel like burning, nausea, fullness, and bloating. Alcohol can also relax the valve at the top of the stomach, which makes acid reflux and heartburn more likely. If nausea is your main morning-after problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) goes deeper on that.

### Digestion slows down

Alcohol can change how fast your stomach empties and how your intestines move. A heavy meal eaten late at night alongside several drinks may sit in your stomach longer than usual, adding to that heavy, stretched feeling. Alcohol also affects the balance of bacteria in your gut over time, which we cover in our guide to [alcohol and digestive health](/never-hungover/alcohol-digestive-health-gi-impact-guide-2025).

### The late-night food effect

Bloating isn't only about the drinks. Greasy, salty, large late-night meals are hard on digestion, and they add the sodium that causes water retention. A lot of "alcohol bloat" is really "alcohol plus pizza at 1 a.m." bloat.

## How Long Does Alcohol Bloating Last?

For a social drinker after a typical night out, facial puffiness usually fades over the course of the next day as you rehydrate, move around, and your body rebalances its fluid and salt. Most people notice a big improvement by the afternoon. Stomach bloating from gas often settles within a day too, though irritation of the stomach lining can leave you feeling off for a bit longer.

There's no exact number of hours that applies to everyone, and anyone who quotes one is guessing. It depends on how much you drank, what you ate, how well you slept, and your own body.

**If the puffiness lasts more than a couple of days, keeps coming back even when you haven't been drinking, or is getting worse, that's a reason to see a doctor.** Ongoing facial swelling can have causes that have nothing to do with a night out, including thyroid problems, kidney problems, allergies, and some medicines.

## How to Get Rid of a Puffy Face After Drinking

None of these is a miracle fix, but together they help your body do what it's already trying to do: clear the extra fluid and settle down.

### Rehydrate steadily, not all at once

Drink water through the morning instead of chugging a liter in five minutes. Plain water is fine for most people. If you were sick or sweated a lot, a drink with electrolytes (sodium and potassium) can help you hold on to fluid where your body needs it. Our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers the timing.

It can seem backward to drink more water to reduce swelling, but it works. When you're well hydrated, your body has less reason to hold on to fluid.

### Eat potassium, go easy on salt

Potassium helps balance sodium and encourages your kidneys to let go of extra fluid. Good sources include bananas, potatoes, sweet potatoes, avocado, spinach, beans, yogurt, oranges, and tomatoes. [Coconut water](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) is another option that's naturally high in potassium.

At the same time, skip the extra salt for the day. That means going easy on bacon, processed meats, salty snacks, instant noodles, and fast food. A classic greasy hangover breakfast may feel good, but it will usually keep the puffiness around longer.

**Note:** if you have kidney disease or take medicines that affect potassium (some blood pressure drugs and diuretics, for example), ask your doctor before loading up on potassium-rich foods or drinks.

### Cool your face down

Cold makes blood vessels narrow and can reduce swelling for a while. Options include:

- Splashing cold water on your face
- A cold, damp washcloth over your eyes for a few minutes
- Chilled spoons or a cool gel eye mask
- A bag of frozen peas wrapped in a thin towel (never put ice directly on your skin)

The effect is real but temporary. It's a good trick if you need to look presentable this morning. It doesn't speed up the underlying recovery much.

### Get upright and move

Gravity and movement both help drain fluid. Sitting up, taking a shower, and going for a short walk get things moving. A gentle face massage, working from the center of your face outward and down toward your neck, may help some fluid drain, though the support for it comes mostly from practical experience rather than research.

### Caffeine in moderation

A cup of coffee or tea can make you feel more alert, and some eye creams include caffeine because it can briefly tighten the look of puffy skin. Don't overdo it, though. A lot of caffeine on top of a hangover can make anxiety, a racing heart, and an upset stomach worse.

### Sleep it off properly next time

Tonight, sleep with your head slightly raised on an extra pillow, and try sleeping on your back. That gives fluid less chance to pool in your face. Getting a full night of sleep without alcohol is one of the most reliable ways to look normal again.

### What to skip

- **Diuretic pills or "water pills"** you weren't prescribed. You're already short on fluid, and these can throw off your electrolytes.
- **More alcohol.** "Hair of the dog" just delays the recovery.
- **Antihistamines "for the puffiness"** while alcohol is still in your system. Many cause drowsiness, and alcohol makes that worse. If you think you're having an allergic reaction, that's a different situation, so see the doctor box above.

## How to Relieve Stomach Bloating After Drinking

- **Stop the fizz.** Swap sparkling water, soda, and anything carbonated for still water for the day.
- **Walk.** Light movement helps gas move through your gut. Even ten minutes can make a difference.
- **Try peppermint or ginger tea.** Both are traditional remedies for an unsettled stomach, and peppermint in particular has some research support for gut discomfort. (Peppermint can make reflux worse in some people, so if you have heartburn, ginger may be the better pick.)
- **Eat small, plain meals.** Toast, rice, bananas, eggs, oatmeal, and broth are easier to handle than a big greasy breakfast.
- **Go easy on gassy foods for a day.** Beans, cabbage, broccoli, and onions are healthy, but they can add to gas while your stomach is already irritated.
- **Over-the-counter gas relief.** Simethicone (sold as Gas-X and other brands) breaks up gas bubbles and is generally considered safe for occasional use. Antacids can help if the main problem is heartburn. Read the label and ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines.
- **Be careful with ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin.** These painkillers can irritate the stomach lining, and alcohol already has. If you need one for a headache, take it with food and water and stick to the label dose. Our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the risks.

## How to Drink Without Waking Up Puffy and Bloated

Prevention works better than any morning-after fix. You don't need to give up a night out to look and feel better the next day.

### Choose your drinks with bloating in mind

| Drink type | Bloating factor | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Beer | High | Carbonation plus fermentable carbs |
| Hard seltzer | Moderate to high | Very carbonated, even if low in sugar |
| Sparkling wine / champagne | Moderate to high | Carbonation, and bubbles may speed up alcohol absorption |
| Spirits with soda, tonic, or cola | Moderate | The mixer brings the gas and often sugar |
| Sugary cocktails | Moderate | Sugar, large volumes, sometimes salt rims |
| Still wine | Lower for the stomach | No carbonation, though red wine can cause flushing in sensitive people |
| Spirits neat, on ice, or with still mixers | Lowest for the stomach | No gas, but it's easy to underestimate how much you've had |

Keep in mind that the type of drink matters less than the amount. Ten "low-bloat" drinks will still leave you puffier than two beers.

### Alternate with water

A glass of water between each drink slows your pace and cuts down on overall fluid loss. It's the single simplest habit for both the puffiness and the hangover in general. For more on the habits with the best evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

### Eat a real meal before you drink

Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol gets into your blood. Pick a balanced meal with protein, vegetables, and complex carbs rather than something extremely salty. Then, if you get hungry late at night, choose something lighter than fries and a burger if you can.

### Have a water-and-potassium routine before bed

Before you go to sleep, drink a glass or two of water. A banana or a few sips of coconut water is a reasonable bedtime snack. Put a glass of water by the bed for the night.

### Set a limit that works for you

US dietary guidelines describe moderate drinking as up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men. You don't have to plan every night around that, but noticing how many drinks reliably leave you puffy is useful. For many people, the difference between "fine" and "puffy" is one or two drinks.

## Is a Puffy Face a Sign of a Bigger Problem?

For someone who drinks now and then, a puffy face the morning after is just a hangover symptom. It's worth knowing, though, that ongoing facial swelling in someone who drinks heavily on a regular basis can be a sign of something more.

- **Liver problems.** A liver damaged by long-term heavy drinking can cause fluid to build up in the belly (called ascites) and the legs. Other signs include yellow skin or eyes, easy bruising, and spidery red blood vessels on the skin.
- **Swollen salivary glands.** Long-term heavy drinking can enlarge the parotid glands, which sit in front of the ears. This can give the face a fuller, rounder look along the jaw that doesn't go away after a day or two.
- **Hormone changes.** Heavy, regular drinking can disrupt the body's main stress hormone (cortisol) and, in some people, cause a "pseudo-Cushing" pattern that can include a rounder face.
- **Skin changes.** Over time, alcohol can contribute to persistent redness and broken blood vessels, and it can make conditions like rosacea worse. Our guide on [alcohol and skin health](/never-hungover/alcohol-skin-health-anti-aging-impact-analysis-2025) covers the long-term effects.

These are not things that happen from a wedding or a weekend out. If your face stays puffy for days at a time, or you notice swelling elsewhere in your body, it's worth seeing a doctor and being honest about how much you drink. They can check your liver, kidneys, and thyroid with simple tests.

**One warning bears repeating:** facial swelling that comes on quickly, especially of the lips, tongue, or throat, with hives, wheezing, or trouble breathing, is a possible allergic reaction. Call 911. Don't wait to see if it's "just a hangover."

## Does DHM Help With Alcohol Bloating?

People sometimes ask whether hangover supplements help with puffiness. Here's an honest view.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol and on liver health. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces facial puffiness or stomach bloating specifically. Those come mostly from fluid loss, salt, and carbonation, and the steps above (water, potassium, less salt, fewer bubbles, fewer drinks) address them directly.

Some people use DHM as part of a broader routine for nights when they drink and say they feel better the next day. If you want to try it, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. No supplement replaces water, food, and drinking less.

## The Bottom Line

- A puffy face after drinking mostly comes from fluid shifts: alcohol makes you lose water, salt makes you hold on to it in the wrong places, and lying flat lets it pool in your face.
- Stomach bloating after drinking mostly comes from carbonation, fermentable carbs in beer, and alcohol irritating the stomach lining, often made worse by a big salty late-night meal.
- To fix it: water through the morning, potassium-rich food, less salt, something cold on your face, and a walk. For your stomach, skip the fizz and eat small, plain meals.
- To prevent it: alternate drinks with water, eat a real meal first, choose fewer carbonated drinks, and drink less overall.
- If swelling lasts more than a couple of days, comes with swelling elsewhere, or appears suddenly on your lips, tongue, or throat, get medical help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my face get puffy after drinking alcohol?**

Mostly because of fluid going to the wrong places. Alcohol blocks a hormone that helps your kidneys hold on to water, so you lose fluid during the night. Once the alcohol wears off, your body holds on to water and salt to rebalance, and some of it settles in the loose tissue of your face and around your eyes. Salty bar food, wider blood vessels from alcohol, and lying flat while you sleep all add to it.

**How long does a puffy face last after drinking?**

For a social drinker after a typical night out, it usually fades over the next day as you rehydrate and move around, with most people noticing a big improvement by the afternoon. It depends on how much you drank, what you ate, and how you slept. If puffiness lasts more than a couple of days or keeps coming back without drinking, see a doctor.

**How do I get rid of alcohol bloating in my face fast?**

Drink water steadily through the morning, eat potassium-rich food such as a banana, potatoes, or avocado, and avoid salty food for the day. Use cold water or a cold compress on your face for a few minutes, sit upright, and take a short walk. The cold trick works quickly but only for a while, while hydration and less salt help the underlying cause.

**Why does alcohol make my stomach bloated?**

Carbonated drinks like beer, hard seltzer, and sparkling wine bring gas into your stomach. Beer also has carbohydrates that gut bacteria ferment into more gas. On top of that, alcohol irritates the stomach lining and can slow digestion, and late-night salty, greasy food makes it worse.

**Which alcohol causes the least bloating?**

For stomach bloating, drinks without carbonation, such as still wine or spirits with still mixers or on ice, tend to cause the least gas. Beer and hard seltzer tend to cause the most. For facial puffiness, the amount you drink matters far more than the type, so pacing yourself and drinking water between rounds helps the most.

**Does drinking water help with alcohol bloating?**

Yes. It sounds backward, but when you're dehydrated your body holds on to fluid, and drinking water helps it let go of the extra. Sip steadily rather than drinking a lot at once. If you were sick or sweated a lot, an electrolyte drink can help too.

**Is a puffy face from alcohol a sign of liver damage?**

After an occasional night out, no. It's a common hangover symptom that goes away on its own. Ongoing facial swelling in someone who drinks heavily on a regular basis can be linked to liver problems, swollen salivary glands, or hormone changes. If your face stays puffy for days, or you notice swelling in your belly or legs, yellow skin or eyes, or easy bruising, see a doctor.

**When should I worry about facial swelling after drinking?**

Call 911 if swelling affects your lips, tongue, or throat, or comes with hives, wheezing, or trouble breathing, since that may be an allergic reaction. See a doctor if swelling lasts more than a couple of days, is on one side only, comes with pain or fever, or you also have swelling in your legs or belly.
